# Sorting under Partial Information with Optimal Preprocessing Time via Unified Bound Heaps

Daniel Rutschmann <sup>∗</sup>

**Abstract**

In 1972, Fredman proposes the problem of sorting under partial information: preprocess a directed acyclic graph _G_ with vertex set _X_ so that you can sort _X_ in _O_(log_e(G_)) time, where _e(G_) is the number of sorted orders compatible with _G_. Cardinal, Fiorini, Joret, Jungers and Munro [S’10] show that you can preprocess _G_ in _O(n_<sup>2.5</sup>) time and then sort _X_ in _O_(log_e(G_)+_n_) time and _O_(log_e(G_)) comparisons. Recent work of van der Hoog and Rutschmann [FOCS’24] implies an algorithm with \(O(n^\omega)\) preprocessing time where \(\omega<2.372\) and _O_(log_e(G_)) sorting time. Haeupler, Hladík, Iacono, Rozhoň, Tarjan and Tˇtek [SODA’25] achieve an overall running time of _O_(log_e(G_)+_m_). In this paper, we achieve tight bounds for this problem: _O(m_) preprocessing time and _O_(log_e(G_)) sorting time.

As a key ingredient, we design a new fast heap data structure that might be of independent theoretical interest. Our heap satisfies the _unified bound_, which has previously been studied for dictionaries and binary search trees.

## 1 Introduction

Comparison based sorting is a fundamental problem in computer science. You are given a list _X_ of _n_ items with some unknown linear order _L_. You can obtain information about _L_ by comparing any pair of items, and the goal is to output _X_ sorted along _L_. Since there are _n!_ possible outputs, an information theoretic lower bound implies that any algorithm needs to do \(\Omega(nlogn)\) comparisons in the worst case. Many textbook sorting algorithms (heapsort, mergesort, deterministic quicksort) match this bound.

In 1976, Fredman \[12\] introduces a generalization of sorting, called _sorting under partial information_: In addition to the list _X_ with unknown linear order _L_, you are given a directed acyclic graph (DAG) _G_ with vertex set _X_, and the promise that every edge \(x\rightarrow y\) of _G_ satisfies _x\<<sub>L</sub>y_. Given this generalized input, the sorting under partial information problem asks: Can you use this DAG to do fewer comparisons? Let _m_ be the number of edges in _G_ and let _e(G_) be the number of linear orders compatible with _G_. An information theoretic lower bound shows that any algorithm needs to do \(\Omega(loge(G))\) comparisons in the worst case. Fredman asks whether this bound is tight. That is, given _G_, can you construct a decision tree of height _O_(log_e(G_)) that sorts _X_?

This setting is very general: If _G_ contains a Hamilton path, then _e(G_)=1, so the decision tree should perform no comparisons after analyzing _G_. If _G_ consists of two disjoint paths of length _n/_2, then \(loge(G)\in\Theta(n)\) and this is the merge problem. If _G_ contains no edges, then \(loge(G)\in\Theta(nlogn)\) and we are back at the vanilla sorting problem. If _G_ is an arbitrary DAG, then _O_(log_e(G_)) can be any value from _O_(1) to _O(n_log_n_).

### Previous work.

In 1976, Fredman \[12\] introduces the problem of sorting under partial information. Given _G_, he shows that you can construct a decision tree of height _O_(log_e(G_)+_n_) that sorts _X_. This exceeds the \(\Omega(loge(G))\) lower bound by an additive _O(n_) term. In 1984, Kahn and Saks \[21\] show that you can construct a decision tree of height _O_(log_e(G_)), matching the information theoretic lower bound. When implemented as a word RAM algorithm, both of their approaches need exponential time to construct the decision tree. This decision tree can then be simulated in _O_(log_e(G_)+_n_) or _O_(log_e(G_)) time, respectively.

Cardinal, Fiorini, Joret, Jungers and Munro \[4\] study this problem algorithmically. They observe that the algorithmic equivalent of constructing a decision tree is a two-stage process: In the _preprocessing phase_, the algorithm can access _G_ but cannot do any comparisons yet. Afterwards, there is a _sorting phase_ where the algorithm can do comparisons. At the end of the sorting phase, the algorithm has to output _X_ sorted along _L_. When the decision tree arguments by Fredman \[12\] and Kahn and Saks \[21\] are converted to algorithms that match this framework, these algorithms need exponential time and space in the preprocessing phase, but achieve a fast sorting phase. Kahn and Kim 1992 \[20\] design the first polynomial time algorithm that sorts _X_ in _O_(log_e(G_)) comparisons. Cardinal, Fiorini, Joret, Jungers and Munro \[4\] show that you can preprocess _G_ in _O(n_<sup>2.5</sup>) time, after which you can sort _X_ in _O_(log_e(G_)) comparisons and _O_(log_e(G_)+_n_) time. The sorting phase of their algorithm can be seen as a decision tree of height _O_(log_e(G_)) that can be implemented by a word RAM algorithm using _O_(log_e(G_)+_n_) time and space.

For all the above algorithms, it doesn’t really matter how we represent _G_ in the input. There are two reasonable choices: For graph algorithms, we typically assume a representation in _O(m_) space, such as a list of _m_ edges, or an adjacency list. But mathematically speaking, the information encoded by _G_ is a partial order on the set _X_, where we can query for any pair \(x,y\in X\) whether \(x\prec y\), similar to an in-memory adjacency matrix. The main difference between these representations is that partial orders are transitively closed: if \(u\prec v\) and \(v\prec w\), then also \(u\prec w\). Directed acyclic graphs need not have this property: there might be edges \(u\rightarrow v\) and \(v\rightarrow w\), but no edge \(u\rightarrow w\).<tbc>

<tbc>We can compute the transitive closure of a directed acyclic graph in \(O(n^\omega)\) time, where \(\omega<2.372\) is the exponent of fast matrix multiplication. Since \(\omega<2.5\), this additional step does not increase the running time of the above algorithms. But for the algorithms below, this does make a difference.

If _G_ is given as a partial order in memory, Van der Hoog and Rutschmann \[19\] achieve \(O(n^{1+\varepsilon})\) preprocessing time and \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}loge(G))\) sorting time, which is tight for this input model. If _G_ is given as a DAG, then we first compute the transitive closure, and then run their algorithm. In the two phase algorithmic framework, this implies an algorithm with \(O(n^\omega)\) preprocessing time that then sorts _X_ in _O_(log_e(G_)) comparisons and time. If we insist on _O_(log_e(G_)) sorting time, then this is the fastest known preprocessing time.

Haeupler, Hladík, Iacono, Rozhoň, Tarjan and Tětek \[14\] and van der Hoog, Rotenberg and Rutschmann \[30\] study the model where _G_ is given as a DAG. They design an algorithm with _O(m_) preprocessing time and _O_(log_e(G_)+_m_) sorting time. This is tight in terms of the _overall running time_. However, compared to previous algorithms, this does not achieve a sorting time of _O_(log_e(G_)). In this paper, we close this gap. We design an algorithm that preprocesses _G_ in _O(m_) time and then sorts _X_ in _O_(log_e(G_)) comparisons and time, which is tight. See  1.

## Further related work

In the geometric setting, algorithms with separate preprocessing and sorting phases have been extensively studied under the _preprocessing model of uncertainty_. Van der Hoog, Kostitsyna, Löffler and Speckmann \[28\] show that you can preprocess a set of intervals in _O(n_log_n_) time, and then, given an item from each interval, sort these items in _O_(log_e(G_)) time, where _G_ is the DAG induced by the intervals. Their result could be seen as the geometric analogue of sorting under partial information. They generalize this to two dimensions \[29\]. Held and Mitchell \[15\] show that you can preprocess a set of disjoint disks in _O(n_log_n_) time, and then, given a point from each disk compute some triangulation in linear time. In the same setting, you can also compute the Gabriel graph, Euclidean MST, Delaunay triangulation (Löffler and Snoeyink \[25\], Devillers \[8\]), or quad tree (Löffler and Mulzer \[23\]) in linear time after preprocessing; or a _k_- layer onion decomposition (Löffler and Mulzer \[24\]) in _O(n_log_k_) time after preprocessing. There are further generalizations to overlapping regions \[1\], regions of arbitrary shape \[32\], or points on lines \[11\].

## Adaptive heap data structures

A heap is a data structure that maintains a set of _n_ comparable items under two operations: insert(_x_) adds a new item to the set, and \(x\leftarrow\text{extractMin}()\) removes the smallest item _x_ from the set and returns this item. Some heaps additionally support the operation decreaseKey(_x,y_), which replaces the item _x_ by an item _y_ with _y\<x_. We require that insert runs in _O_(1) (amortized) time and then seek to minimize the running time of extractMin. We say a heap is adaptive if extractMin runs in _o_(log_n_) time for specific sequences of insert and extractMin operations. Adaptive data structures are useful since they allow us to perform \(\Theta(n)\) operations while still achieving a sorting time of _o(n_log_n_).

Iacono \[17\] shows that the pairing heap has the _working set bound_: It supports \(x\leftarrow\text{extractMin}()\) in _O_(log_k_) time where _k_ is the number of insert operations performed while _x_ is in the heap. By using this result, Haeupler, Hladík, Iacono, Rozhoň, Tarjan and Tětek \[14\] obtain their _O_(log_e(G_)+_m_) algorithm for sorting under partial information. Recently, adaptive heap data structures have led to fast algorithms for other problems: Haeupler, Hladík, Rozhoň, Tarjan and Tětek \[13\] design a heap data structure with the working set bound that also supports the decrease-key operation in _O_(1) amortized time. They show that Dijkstra’s algorithm with their heap is universally optimal.

Furthermore, Elmasry \[9\] designs a heap that supports \(x\leftarrow\text{extractMin}()\) in _O_(log_k_) time where _k_ is the number of items that get inserted after _x_ and remain in the heap until _x_ gets extracted. Elmasry, Farzan and Iacono \[10\] design a heap that supports \(x\leftarrow\text{extractMin}()\) in \(O(min(logk,log\ell))\) time where _k_ is defined the same way and \(\ell\) is the number of items that get inserted _before x_ and remain in the heap until _x_ gets extracted. Kozma and Saranurak \[22\] introduce the _smooth heap_, which is conjectured to be instance optimal, but seems difficult to analyze.

## Contribution.

We provide the first algorithm for sorting under partial information that is tight in both preprocessing and sorting time. To this end, we introduce the notion of the _unified bound_ for heaps. Consider an initially empty heap under insert and extractMin operations. We allow some items to remain in the heap at the end of the execution. Let _X_ be the set of items that get inserted into the heap. For an item \(x\in X\), let \(a(x)\in[n]\) denote the number of items that get inserted no later than _x_ gets inserted. If _x_ does not get extracted, put \(b(x)=\infty\), otherwise, let \(b(x)\in[n]\) denote the number of items that get extracted no later than _x_ gets extracted. In other words, _x_ is the _a(x_)-th item to be inserted, and the _b(x_)-th item to be extracted.

**Definition 1.** _A heap data structure has the_ unified bound _if it supports_ insert(_x_) _in amortized O_(1) _time, the very first_ extractMin _operation in amortized O_(1) _time, and subsequent_ \(x\leftarrow\text{extractMin}()\) _operations in amortized time_

\(O\big(min_{y\in Xb(y)<b(x)}\big(1+log|a(x)-a(y)|+log(b(x)-b(y)))\big)\big).\)

Intuitively, the unified bound allows us to use items _y_ that were already extracted as a "finger" to find the item _x_ that gets extracted next. The cost of using a particular item _y_ contains two terms: log|_a(x_)-_a(y_)|, and log(_b(x_)-_b(y_)). Roughly speaking, log|_a(x_)-_a(y_)| measures how "close" _x_ and _y_ are in the insertion order, while log(_b(x_)-_b(y_)) measures how "old" the finger _y_ is. Crucially, we do not need to specify _y_ ourselves; the data structure automatically selects an (asymptotically) optimal _y_. Designing a heap with the unified bound is our main technical contribution:

**Theorem 2.** _There is a heap data structure with the unified bound._

We believe that this data structure and our notion of heaps with the unified bound are of independent theoretical interest. For example, we show:

**Lemma 3** (Informal Lemma 8)**.** _If a heap has the unified bound, then it also has the working set property._

Next, we use this heap to design a fast algorithm for sorting under partial information. Let `UniTopSort` be the following two-phase algorithm: In the preprocessing phase, `UniTopSort` computes a topological ordering of _G_. This is the only preprocessing step, and takes _O(n+m_) time. In the sorting phase, `UniTopSort` considers all items of _X_ in topological order and inserts them into a heap with the unified bound. Then, it repeatedly extracts the minimum from the heap. This yields _X_ in sorted order. Note that, to perform the insert and extractMin operations, the heap has to compare items. But this is fine, since we have access to the linear order _L_ in the sorting phase. _A priori_, it seems unlikely that `UniTopSort` achieves _O_(log_e(G_)+_n_) sorting time. Indeed, the only information about the graph _G_ that `UniTopSort` retains is a topological ordering. Surprisingly, we show:

**Theorem 4.** _`UniTopSort` has O(n+m_) _preprocessing time and O_(log_e(G_)+_n_) _sorting time._

From Theorem 4, we apply existing reductions to reduce the preprocessing time to _O(m_) and the sorting time to _O_(log_e(G_)). The sorting time bounds the number of comparisons. This yields:

**Theorem 5.** _We can preprocess a DAG G on X in O(m_) _time, so that, given an unknown linear order L on X and the guarantee that all edges in G go from smaller items to larger items with respect to L, we can sort X in O_(log_e(G_)) _time and comparisons._

### Comparison to existing algorithms for DAG sorting

Both `UniTopSort` and the algorithm of Haeupler, Hladík, Iacono, Rozhoň, Tarjan and Tětek \[14\] are variants of Heapsort that use an adaptive heap data structure guided by a topological ordering of _G_. Thus, at a surface level, these algorithms might look similar. However, the two algorithms operate very differently. Let us illustrate three key differences:

(1) The algorithm of \[14\] tries to keep the heap as small as possible, by inserting items on the fly once they become relevant (i.e. become sources in _G_). Thus, the algorithm interleaves insert and extractMin operations. `UniTopSort` inserts all _n_ items into the heap immediately.

(2) The algorithm of \[14\] is closely tied to the graph _G_: Whenever an item is extracted from the heap, the algorithm looks at all outgoing edges from that item. This yields the _O(m_) term in the sorting time. `UniTopSort` does not care about the individual edges of _G_ beyond using them to find a topological ordering of _G_.

(3) The heap used by \[14\] is much simpler than the one we use: You can obtain a heap with the working set via a simple bucket-based construction with heaps of exponentially increasing sizes \[31\]. Our construction of a heap with the unified bound is involved. We have reasons to believe that an involved construction is necessary, as the cost function in the unified bound contains two separate terms (log|_a(x_)-_a(y_)| and log(_b(x_)-_b(y_))). We discuss prior attempts at this in Section 2.2.

The other existing algorithms for DAG sorting do not use heaps: \[30\] use a variant of insertion sort with a finger search tree, where they look at all outgoing edges of an item to determine the optimal finger. \[4\] and \[19\] decompose the graph into paths and use a variant of merge sort based on Huffman trees.

## 2 Preliminaries

We denote \[_n_\]={1,2_,...,n_} and we use log for the base-2 logarithm. Let _X_ be the set of items and let _G_ be a DAG with vertex set _X_. We say a linear order _L_ on _X_ is _compatible with G_ if all edges in _G_ go from a smaller item to a larger item under _L_, that is, _x\<<sub>L</sub>y_ for every edge \(x\rightarrow y\).

## 2.1 Existing Machinery for Sorting under Partial Information

The interval lemma is a powerful tool for analysing fast algorithms that use adaptive data structures. It was originally introduced in \[4\] and has been extensively used \[4,13,14,19,30\]. Here, we consider a lopsided version where the number of intervals may be different from the range of the intervals. For example, for the analysis in Section 3, it is convenient to consider _n_ intervals in \[1,2_n_\].

**Lemma 6** (A generalization of Lemma 3.2 in \[4\])**.** _Let_ \(\{[a_i,b_i]\}_{i=1}^k\) _be a family of k subintervals of_ \[0_,m_\] _that each have size at least_ 1_. Let Z be the set of linear orders realizable by real numbers_ \(z_i\in[a_i,b_i]\)_. Then_ \(\sum_{i\in[k]}log(b_i-a_i)\in O(klog(\frac{em}{k})+log|Z|)\).

_Proof._ Many existing proofs of Lemma 3.2 in \[4\] can be adapted to work in the lopsided setting. For example, we tweak the proof of \[14\]: For each _i_ between 1 and _k_ inclusive, choose a real number _z<sub>i</sub>_ uniformly at random from the real interval \[0_,m_\], independently for each _i_. With probability 1, the _z<sub>i</sub>_ are distinct. Let _L_ be the permutation of \[_k_\] obtained by sorting \[_k_\] by _z<sub>i</sub>_. Each possible permutation is equally likely. If each \(z_i\in[a_i,b_i]\) then _L_ is in _Z_. The probability of this happening is \(\prod_{i=1}^k\frac{b_i-a_i}{m}\) . It follows that \(|Z|\ge k!\cdot\prod_{i=1}^k\frac{b_i-a_i}{m}\) . Taking logarithms gives \(log|Z|\ge\sum_{i=1}^klog(b_i-a_i)+logk!-klogm\). By Stirling’s approximation of the factorial, \(logk!\ge klogk-kloge\). Thus,

\(\sum_{i=1}^klog(b_i-a_i)\le log|Z|+klogm-logk!\le log|Z|+klog\left(\frac{em}{k}\right).\square\)

In the introduction, we present two algorithms for sorting under partial information with different running times: Theorem 4 and Theorem 5. The main difference between these is the additional _O(n_) term in the sorting time of Theorem 4. This term is only relevant if \(loge(G)\in o(n)\), and there is existing machinery \[4,19,30\] for dealing with this case: Roughly speaking, this can only happen if there is a very long path in _G_. We can find this path during the preprocessing phase, and not waste any comparisons on it during the sorting phase. Formally:

**Lemma 7** (Lemma 1 in \[30\] + Lemma 8 of \[19\])**.** _Let P be a longest path in G. Then,_ \(n-|P|\in O(loge(G))\)_. Moreover, after performing O(n+m_) _preprocessing on G, we can, given the sorted order of X-P, sort all of X in O_(log_e(G_)) _time during the sorting phase._

In Section 4 we use this lemma to derive Theorem 5 from Theorem 4.

## 2.2 Existing Results on Adaptive Data Structures

In this paper, we mainly focus on adaptive heap data structures. However, there is a standard way of using a binary search tree as a heap: sort the items by the order in which they were inserted, and maintain the subtree minimum at each node. Thus, we will also mention some results on binary search trees, as these results have implications for adaptive heaps.

### Existing notions of unified bounds.

Unified bounds were first defined for binary search trees. For splay trees, Sleator and Tarjan \[26\] use the term "unified bound" for the minimum of three other bounds, the so-called static optimality, static finger, and working set bound. However, Elmasry, Farzan and Iacono \[10\] show that this "unified bound" is equivalent to the working set bound. Hence, this definition has been obsoleted.

Iacono \[18\] introduces the unified bound for binary search trees, which is strictly stronger than the working set bound for binary search trees. He conjectures that the splay tree also satisfies this<tbc>

<tbc>stronger bound. This terminology is also used in \[2,3\]. Elmasry, Farzan and Iacono \[10\] attempt to define a unified bound for Heaps, based on Iacono’s \[18\] unified bound for binary search trees. They use the term "unified conjecture" for this bound. Their "unified conjecture" bound, using our notation from Definition 1, is \(min_{y\in X:b(y)<b(x)}\big(1+log|\text{rank}(x)-\text{rank}(y)|+log(b(x)-b(y)))\), where rank(_x_) is the number of items currently in the heap that are smaller than _x_. Unfortunately, they show that, if a heap supports insert in amortized _O_(1) time, the running time of \(x\leftarrow\text{extractMin}()\) cannot be within the "unified conjecture".

Definition 1 avoids this obstruction, since it uses the insert time _a(x_) instead of the rank, and has an additional nice property: If you use a binary search tree that has the unified bound (in the sense of Iacono \[18\]) as a heap, the resulting heap has the unified bound (in the sense of Definition 1)<sup>1</sup>.

## Existing heaps fall short of the unified bound.

None of the existing heap data structures \[9, 10,17\] mentioned in the introduction are known to have the unified bound. It is conceivable that the smooth heap or (some variant of) the pairing heap has the unified bound - we see this as an interesting but difficult open problem.

As discussed above, transforming a binary search tree with the unified bound into a heap would yield a heap with the unified bound. Unfortunately, there are no known binary search tree data structures with the unified bound. The splay tree is conjectured to have the unified bound \[18\], but this conjecture remains open. Resolving the dynamic finger conjecture for the splay tree took considerable effort \[5\], and the unified bound would imply this conjecture. The binary search tree data structure of Derryberry and Sleator \[7\] has an additive _O_(loglog_n_) overhead on top of the unified bound. This would raise the running time of `UniTopSort` to _O(n_loglog_n_+log_e(G_)). The dictionaries without this overhead \[2,3,18\] cannot be transformed into a heap, as they are not binary search trees. Thus, there is no easy way of obtaining a heap with the unified bound.

## Comparing the unified bound and the working set bound for heaps.

For some sequences of insert and extractMin operations, the unified bound is strictly stronger than the working set bound: Consider inserting the items 1_,n_+1,2_,n_+2_,...,n,_2_n_ into a heap, and then repeatedly calling extractMin until the heap is empty. A heap with the unified bound can perform these operations in _O(n_) total time, while the working set bound is only _O(n_log_n_). Conversely, we now prove Lemma 3: if a heap has the unified bound, then it automatically has the working set property.

**Lemma 8.** _If a heap has the unified bound, then the_ insert _operation runs in amortized constant time, and the_ \(x\leftarrow\text{extractMin}()\) _operation runs in amortized O_(1+log(1+_t-a(x_))) _time, where t is the number of_ insert _operations performed so far and a(x_) _is as in Definition 1._

Note that _t-a(x_) is the number of insert operations that were performed while _x_ is in the heap, so _O_(1+log(1+_t-a(x_))) is indeed the working set bound.

_Proof._ Consider an arbitrary sequence _S_ of _t_ insert operations and _k_ extractMin operations. This takes _O(n+m_) time using a textbook algorithm. In the sorting phase of `UniTopSort`, every item in _X_ gets inserted and extracted exactly once. In the remainder of this section, we will prove Theorem 12. ## 5.1 Overview At a high level, our data structure consists of two parts. First, the _main tree_: a complete binary tree with \(\Theta(n)\) leaves, ordered by index. Some nodes in this tree are _leaders_, where every leaf _i_ lies in the subtree of exactly one leader. We call this leader the _leader of leaf i_. Second, the _index trees_: we store the leaders in _O_(loglog_n_) balanced binary search trees of doubly exponential sizes. Each index tree is ordered by the left-to-right order of the leaders in the main tree. From the main tree and the index trees, we obtain a single tree, as required by Theorem 12, as follows: connect the roots of the index trees from big to small, and attach to each leader node in the index tree its subtree in the main tree. This yields some nodes with three children, but we can subdivide these nodes to get a binary tree. (This increases the depth of each leaf by at most a factor 2.) In Theorem 12, leaf _i_ should have depth _O(d(i_)). Thus, in our construction, for any leaf _i_ with leader _v_, both the height of the subtree of _v_ in the main tree, and the height of the index tree that contains _v_ should be bounded by _O(d(i_)). We will implement the access(_i_) operation by moving the leaders down in the main tree, with the goal that leaf _i_ ends up at depth _O_(1). Our carefully chosen invariants then guarantee that nearby leaves _j_ also have depth _O(d(j_)). We implement an additional operation cleanup that moves the leaders up in the main tree, with the goal of reducing the size of the index trees. We invoke cleanup() after every addLeaf or access operation. Finally, it is easy to implement changeKey: since the values of items have no effect on the shape of our structure, we just update all subtree minima on the root-to-leaf path. The main difficulty is maintaining the subtree minima in the index trees as we create and destroy leaders: while there are balanced binary trees with _O_(1) insertion or deletion after lookup, updating the subtree minima will take time linear in the height of the index tree. To deal with this, we use a charging argument where we insert log_S_ consecutive leaders into an index tree at once, where _S_ is the size of the index tree. Then, updating the subtree minima only takes _O_(1) time per leader inserted.

## 5.2 Invariants

We first describe the _main tree M_: This is a complete binary tree with \(m\in[n+1,2n]\) leaves, numbered 1,2_,...,m_ where _m_ is some power of two. The first _n_ of these leaves store items as in Theorem 12, while the remaining leaves are there for future addLeaf operations. Recall the definition of _t,s(i_) and _d(i_). We say the _height_ of a node is the height of its subtree in _M_. (Leaves have height 0.) Our goal is to maintain a set of leader nodes so that, for every _i_, the subtree of the leader of leaf _i_ has height _O(d(i_)). To this end, every node in _M_ can be _active_ or _passive_. We say a node _u_ is a _leader_ if _u_ is active and the parent of _u_ is passive. We require the following invariants:

(1) The leaves 1_,...,n_ are active, and the leaves _n_+1_,...m_ are passive.<tbc>

(2) If a node is active, then its children are active.<tbc>

(3) Consecutive leaders have a height difference of at most two. Formally: Let _u_<sub>1</sub>_,u_<sub>2</sub>_,..._ be the leaders in left to right order. Then \(|\text{height}(u_j)-\text{height}(u_{j+1})|\le 2\) for every _j_.<tbc>

(4) For every leaf _i_, the \(\lceil log_2(1+t-s(i))\rceil\)-th ancestor of _i_ is passive.<tbc>

(5) The parent of leaf _n_ is passive.

We will soon add some additional invariants to guarantee that the number of leaders stays small. Indeed, with just the invariants (1)-(5), we could make every leaf its own leader. However, we first show that these invariants already imply that the depth of each leaf is within the unified bound.

**Lemma 13.** _Every active node (and each leaf_ 1_,...,n) lies in the subtree of a unique leader._

_Proof._ We first show that the root of _M_ is passive. Indeed, since \(m\ge(n+1)\), the leaf _n_+1 exists. By invariant (1), this leaf is passive, so by invariant (2), the root of _M_ is passive too.

Let _u_ be an arbitrary active node. In particular, by invariant (1), _u_ could be any leaf of index 1_,...,n_. Let _v_ be the first active node on a root-to-_u_ path. By invariant (2), all nodes after _v_ are active. We have seen that _v_ cannot be the root of _M_. Thus, by definition, _v_ is the only leader on the root-to-_u_ path.

Invariants (3) and (4) imply that the depth of each leaf is bounded by the unified bound:

**Lemma 14.** _Let v be the leader of the i-th leaf. Then_ \(\text{height}(v)\le d(i)+3\).

_Proof._ Let _u,v,w_ be consecutive leaders, that is, in left to right order, let _u_ be the leader before _v_, and let _w_ be the leader after _v_. By invariant (3), \(\text{height}(u)\ge\text{height}(v)-2\) and \(\text{height}(w)\ge\text{height}(v)-2\). In particular, if \(|j-i|\le 2^{\text{height}(v)-2}\), then the _j_-th leaf lies in one of the subtrees of _u,v,w_, so by invariant (4), we have \(1+t-s(j)\ge 2^{\text{height}(v)-3}\). For all other _j_, we have \(|j-i|\ge 2^{\text{height}(v)-2}\). Therefore, \(d(i)=1+min_{1\le j\le n}(log(1+|i-j|)+log(1+t-s(j)))\ge\text{height}(v)-3\).

The astute reader might notice that we have not used invariant (5) so far. Indeed, (5) will only be used to support addLeaf in _O_(1) time, where it allows us to activate leaf _n_+1 without violating invariants (2) or (4).

We now describe the index trees _L_<sub>0</sub>_,L_<sub>1</sub>_,..._. Each index tree _L<sub>i</sub>_ is a balanced binary search tree. Every leader is stored in exactly one index tree, and leaders in the same index tree are ordered by their left-to-right order in the main tree _M_. These index trees have additional invariants:

(6) Before every addLeaf or access operation, the size of _L<sub>i</sub>_ is at most \(20\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\). After an addLeaf or access operation, the size of _L<sub>i</sub>_ is at most \(23\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\).<tbc>

(7) All leaders in _L_<sub>0</sub> have a height in \[0,4\], and for \(i\ge 1\), all leaders in _L<sub>i</sub>_ have a height in \([2^i,4\cdot 2^i]\). (Recall that the height of a leader is its height in _M_, not in _L<sub>i</sub>_.)<tbc>

(8) The leaders in _L<sub>i</sub>_ of height \((2\cdot 2^i,4\cdot 2^i]\) in _L<sub>i</sub>_ are called _unpromoted_. Among every maximal sequence \(u_\ell,\dots,u_r\) of consecutive leaders in _M_ that all are in _L<sub>i</sub>_ and are all unpromoted, we require there be at least one leader of height \(2\cdot 2^i+1\) or \(2\cdot 2^i+2\). We call such a sequence \(u_\ell,\dots,u_r\) an _unpromoted block_.

Invariant (8) might seem artificial at first, but it will allow us to move many leaders from _L<sub>i</sub>_ to _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub> at once. Indeed, whenever there is a leader of height \(4\cdot 2^i\) in _L<sub>i</sub>_, the unpromoted block in invariant (8) contains \(\Omega(2^i)\) consecutive unpromoted leaders in _M_. By promoting a whole block from _L<sub>i</sub>_ to _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>, we will save a bunch of time updating subtree minima. Invariants (6) and (7) allow us to bound the height of the index trees:

**Lemma 15.** _Let u be a leader that is stored in some index tree L<sub>i</sub>. Then_ \(\text{height}(L_i)\in O(\text{height}(u))\).

_Proof._ By Invariant (7), we have \(\text{height}(u)\ge 2^i\) or _i_=0. By Invariant (6) and (7), we have \(|L_i|\le 23\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\). Thus, \(\text{height}(L_i)\le 2^{i+2}log(4)+log(23)\in O(2^i)\).

## 5.3 Storing the data structure

We use a "level-linked" representation of the main tree: every node stores pointers to its parent and its children, plus pointers to the left and right neighbor of the same height. Every internal node stores a Boolean indicating whether it is active or not. Every leaf _i_ stores its index _i_, its item, and its last access time _s(i_). Each active internal node moreover stores the maximum access time in its subtree, and a pointer to the minimum item in its subtree. In combination with invariant (3), this level-linked representation allows us to go from a leader to the next or previous leader by following _O_(1) pointers and checking whether _O_(1) nodes are active or not.

For the index trees, we use any balanced binary tree that allows us to insert or delete _k_ (presorted) consecutive items in _O(k_+log_S_) time where _S_ is the size of the balanced binary tree. We call this a _bulk insertion / deletion_. If a balanced binary tree _T_ of size _S_ can be built in _O(S_) time and supports split and join operations in _O_(log_S_), then we can do a bulk insertion by splitting _T_ into _T_<sub>1</sub>_,T_<sub>2</sub> at the insertion location, building a tree \(T'\) on the _k_ presorted elements, and joining \(T_1,T',T_2\). Similarly, we can perform a bulk deletion by splitting _T_ into \(T_1,T',T_2\) and joining _T_<sub>1</sub>_,T_<sub>2</sub>. One example of a balanced binary tree with these properties is a red-black tree \[27\].

Every node in an index tree stores its subtree minimum, and the size of its subtree. We can update these values during a split or join operation in _O_(log_S_) time. In particular, while maintaining these values, we can still do bulk insertions and bulk deletion in _O(k_+log_S_) time. For every leader, we store pointers between its node in the main tree and its node in the index trees.

## 5.4 Amortized Analysis Potential

We use the accounting method \[6\]: creating a coin or bill takes _O_(1) amortized time, you can spend a coin to do _O_(1) work for free, and spend a bill to gain _O_(1) coins. We have the following money:

• two coins per leader node,<tbc>

• one additional coin per unpromoted leader node, and<tbc>

• one bill per pair of consecutive leaders with height difference 2.

We think it is easier to keep track of money locally. But, for readers that prefer working with potential functions, you may think of the potential function

\(\Phi=(\text{total number of coins})+10^9\cdot(\text{total number of bills}).\)

## 5.5 The access operation

Recall that a leader is an active node in the main tree with an inactive parent. We perform access in two steps. First, we ignore the index trees and only update the main tree. We deactivate a bunch of nodes, which changes the set of leaders. Second, we bulk delete the destroyed leaders from the index trees, and bulk insert the newly created leaders into the index trees. This approach saves a bunch of time updating subtree minima in the index trees.

To implement access(_i_), first deactivate all non-leaf nodes on the root-to-leaf path of leaf _i_. Then, while there are consecutive leaders _u,v_ with \(\text{height}(u)-\text{height}(v)\ge 3\), deactivate _u_ and the right child of _u_. Similarly, whenever \(\text{height}(v)-\text{height}(u)\ge 3\), deactivate _v_ and the left child of _v_. Finally, erase all destroyed leaders from the index trees, and insert all newly created leaders into the index trees. Inserting or deleting leaders one-by-one would be too slow. Instead, for every _i_=0,1_,..._, we build a linked list _N<sub>i</sub>_ on all newly created leaders of height \((2\cdot 2^i,4\cdot 2^i]\) in left-to-right order, or height \[0,4\] for _i_=0. Then, for each affected index tree _L<sub>i</sub>_, we bulk delete the destroyed leaders from _L<sub>i</sub>_, and bulk insert _N<sub>i</sub>_ into _L<sub>i</sub>_. Note that, except for leaders of height \[0,2\] in _L_<sub>0</sub>, all newly created leaders are unpromoted (invariant (8)).

We now analyze this implementation of access(_i_):

**Lemma 16.** _At any point in time during and after the_ access _operation, the set of newly created leaders is_ contiguous_, that is, it forms a contiguous subsequence of all leaders in the left-to-right order._

_Proof._ Let _w_ be the leader of leaf _i_ before the access operation. First, we deactivate all non-leaf nodes on the path from _w_ to _i_. The newly created leaders are precisely the subset of leaders that lie in the subtree of _w_. Hence, they are contiguous. After that, we always find two consecutive leaders _u,v_ with \(|\text{height}(u)-\text{height}(v)|\ge 3\) and deactivate one of them, say _u_. Note that, since invariant (3) held before the access operation, at least one of _u,v_ has to be a newly created leader. Deactivating _u_ replaces it with two newly created leaders, so the set of newly created leaders remains contiguous.

**Lemma 17.** _At any point in time during and after the_ access(_i_) _operation, the heights of newly created leaders to the left of leaf i are non-increasing, and the heights of newly created leaders to the right of leaf i are non-decreasing. Moreover, at most two consecutive newly created leaders have the same height._

_Proof._ This is true after we deactivate all non-leaf nodes on the root-to-leaf path to node _i_. We show that Lemma 17 is maintained as we deactivate more nodes. Let _t,u,v_ be consecutive leaders with \(\text{height}(u)-\text{height}(v)\ge 3\). By assumption, Lemma 17 holds before we deactivate _u_. Thus, _t_ is either an old leader, or \(\text{height}(t)\ge\text{height}(u)\); and leaf _i_ lies weakly to the right of _v_. We deactivate _u_ and its right child. This replaces _u_ with three new leaders _u_<sub>1</sub>_,u_<sub>2</sub>_,u_<sub>3</sub> with height(_u_<sub>1</sub>)=height(_u_)-1 and height(_u_<sub>2</sub>)=height(_u_<sub>3</sub>)=height(_u_)-2. Thus, \(\text{height}(u_1)>\text{height}(u_2)\ge\text{height}(u_3)>\text{height}(v)\). And, _t_ is either an old leader, or height(_t)\>_height(_u_<sub>1</sub>). Moreover, among _t,u_<sub>1</sub>_,u_<sub>2</sub>_,u_<sub>3</sub>_,v_, only _u_<sub>2</sub> and _u_<sub>3</sub> can be new leaders of the same height. This shows that Lemma 17 still holds after the deactivations, so Lemma 17 is maintained until the end.

**Lemma 18.** _This implementation of_ access(_i_) _correctly maintains all invariants._

_Proof._ We never deactivate leaf nodes, so invariant (1) holds. First, we deactivate all nodes on a root-to-leaf path. After that we only deactivate leader nodes, which by definition have a passive parent. Thus, invariant (2) holds. Whenever there are consecutive leaders _u,v_ with |height(_u_)-<tbc>

<tbc>\(\text{height}(v)|\ge 3\), we deactivate one of them. Thus, invariant (3) holds at the end of access(_i_). Since we do not activate any nodes, invariant (5) is unaffected, and so is invariant (4) for all leaves \(j\neq i\). Since these held before, they still hold afterwards. After access(_i_), we have _s(i_)=_t_-1, so that \(\lceil log(1+t-s(i))\rceil=1\). Since we deactivated the parent of leaf _i_, invariant (4) also holds for leaf _i_.

By Lemma 17, we create at most four leaders of every height. Thus, by invariant (7), we increase the size of _L<sub>i</sub>_ by at most \(4\cdot 4\cdot 2^i\). Since \(20\cdot 4^{2i+2}+4\cdot 4\cdot 2^i\le 23\cdot 4^{2i+2}\), invariant (6) is preserved. We insert only leaders of height \(\le 4\cdot 2^i\) into the index tree _L<sub>i</sub>_. Therefore, invariant (7) holds, and all newly created leaders are unpromoted. Let _u_ be a newly created leader, of height \((2\cdot 2^i,4\cdot 2^i]\). By invariant (3), there is a newly created leader _v_ of height \(2\cdot 2^i+1\) or \(2\cdot 2^i+2\) between _u_ and leaf _i_. By Lemmas 16 and 17, all leaders between _u_ and _v_ have height \((2\cdot 2^i,4\cdot 2^i]\). Thus, invariant (8) is maintained. This shows the lemma.

**Lemma 19.** _The amortized running time of_ access(_i_) _is O(d(i_)).

_Proof._ We first analyze the time spent updating the main tree and the number of coins created. We generalize the notion of bills to larger height differences: A pair _u,v_ of consecutive leaders has max(0,|height(_u_)-height(_v_)|-1) bills. By Lemma 14, the existing leader of leaf _i_ has height _O(d(i_)). Thus, deactivating the nodes on the root-to-leaf path of leaf _i_ takes _O(d(i_)) time and creates _O(d(i_)) bills and coins. Consider now three consecutive leaders _t,u,v_ with height(_u_)-height\((v)\ge 3\). We deactivate _u_ and the right child of _u_. This creates three new leaders _u_<sub>1</sub>_,u_<sub>2</sub>_,u_<sub>3</sub> with height(_u_<sub>1</sub>)=height(_u_)-1 and height(_u_<sub>2</sub>)=height(_u_<sub>3</sub>)=height(_u_)-2. Overall, the number of bills decreases by at least one. Indeed, the pair _u_<sub>3</sub>_,v_ has two fewer bills compared to the pair _u,v_, but the pair _t,u_<sub>1</sub> might have one more bill compared to _t,u_. We use this one bill to pay for the _O_(1) coins of _u_<sub>1</sub>_,u_<sub>2</sub>_,u_<sub>3</sub> and for the _O_(1) time spent.

This shows that the time spent updating the main tree and the number of coins created have an amortized cost of _O(d(i_)). Next, we show that the time spent updating the index trees is _O(k_) where _k_ is the number of newly created leaders. Then, this time is dominated by the time spent updating the main tree, and the lemma follows. Building the linked lists _N<sub>i</sub>_ takes constant time per newly created leader. To analyze the time spent splitting or joining the index trees, let _h_ be the maximum height of any newly created leader. On each of the index trees _L_<sub>0</sub>_,...,L_<sub>_O_(log_h_)</sub>, we perform a bulk deletion and a bulk insertion, involving _O(k_) leaders in total. By Lemma 15, each of these trees has height _O(h_). Moreover, the heights of these trees are bounded by a geometric series. Thus, the bulk operations take _O(k+h_) time in total. By invariant (3) and Lemma 16, there are at least _h/_2 newly created leaders, i.e. \(h\in O(k)\). This shows the lemma.

To summarize, Lemma 18 shows that access(_i_) is correct, and Lemma 19 shows that access(_i_) has the running time required by Theorem 12.

## 5.6 The addLeaf operation

The addLeaf operation is easy to implement: We activate leaf _n_+1 and insert it into the first index tree _L_<sub>0</sub>. Then, we increment _n_. Finally, if _n=m_, then we double _m_ and increase the height of the main tree by 1. All newly created nodes are passive.

Activating leaf _n_+1 makes it a leader. By invariant (5), leaf _n_ is also a leader, so invariant (3) is maintained. We only add one leader to _L_<sub>0</sub>, so invariant (6) is maintained. It is easy to see that all other invariants are maintained.

As for the running time, leaf _n_+1 becomes a new leader, which creates one coin. If we do not double _m_, then addLeaf takes _O_(1) amortized time. Indeed, by invariants (6) and (7), the first index tree _L_<sub>0</sub> has constant height, so inserting the new leader takes constant time. Whenever we<tbc>

<tbc>double _m_, we spend _O(m_) time to create the new nodes. By the standard amortization argument for dynamic arrays \[6\], this amounts to amortized _O_(1) time per addLeaf operation. This shows:

**Theorem 20.** _This implementation of_ addLeaf _correctly maintains all invariants and has an amortized running time of O_(1).

## 5.7 The cleanup operation

We first describe a subroutine cleanupStep(_i_). This subroutine reduces the size of _L<sub>i</sub>_ back to \(\le 16\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\), in amortized zero time, but it might increase the size of _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub> in the process. We achieve this by both moving unpromoted blocks from _L<sub>i</sub>_ to _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>, and by activating as many nodes in the main tree as possible, without violating invariants (4) or (7).

To perform cleanupStep(_i_), first build a linked list _A_ of all leaders in _L_<sub>0</sub>_,...,L<sub>i</sub>_ in left-to-right order. For every leader of height \(4\cdot 2^i\) in _A_, find its unpromoted block of leaders of height \(>2\cdot 2^i\) in _A_, remove the block from _A_ and insert it into _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>. Then, while there are consecutive leaders _t,u,v,w_ where _u,v_ have the same parent _p_, activate _p_ unless (a) \(height(p)>min(height(t),height(w))+1\); (b) this would violate invariant (4) or (5); or (c) \(height(p)>4\cdot 2^i\). If we do activate _p_, replace _u,v_ by _p_ in the linked list. Finally, we rebuild the index trees: For every \(0\le j\le i\), build a balanced binary tree _L<sub>j</sub>_ that contains all (remaining) leaders in _A_ of height \((2\cdot 2^j,4\cdot 2^j]\), or height \[0,4\] for _j_=0. This concludes cleanupStep(_i_).

To efficiently find a parent _p_ to activate during cleanupStep(_i_), we maintain a pointer to the leader _t_ and perform a left-to-right scan through _A_. Whenever we fail to activate _p_, we move this pointer one step to the right. Whenever we successfully activate _p_, we move this pointer two steps to the left. When the pointer reaches the end of _A_, there are no more parents _p_ to activate.

We now describe the full operation cleanup. Recall invariant (6). The goal of cleanup is to reduce the size of all index trees from up to \(23\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\) to at most \(20\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\). To perform cleanup, find the maximum index _i_ with \(|L_i|>20\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\), and call cleanupStep(_i_). Repeat this until no such index _i_ exists. A naive implementation of cleanup spends _O_(loglog_n_) time per iteration looking for the index _i_. We avoid this overhead by keeping all index trees _L<sub>i</sub>_ with \(|L_i|>20\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\) in a linked list and updating this linked list whenever we update an index tree during addLeaf, access, or cleanupStep. With this bookkeeping, the running time of cleanup is _O_(1) plus the time spent calling cleanupStep.

**Lemma 21.** _After_ cleanupStep(_i), for every_ \(k<4\cdot 2^i\)_, there are at most_ \(16\cdot 4^k\) _leaders of height_ \(\le k\)_. And, there are at most_ \(12\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\) _leaders of height exactly_ \(4\cdot 2^i\)_. In particular,_ \(|L_j|\le 16\cdot 4^{2^{j+2}}\) _for every_ \(0\le j\le i\).

_Proof._ We say a leader is _locked_ if its parent cannot be activated due to invariant (4) or (5). We first analyze the number of locked nodes: There are at most two locked nodes of height \(\le k\) for every leaf _i_ with \(\lceil log_2(1+t-s(i))\rceil\le k+1\), or equivalently, \(t-s(i)\le 2^{k+1}-1\). Since the _s(i_) values are pairwise distinct and satisfy _s(i)\<t_, there are at most 2<sup>_k_+1</sup>-1 such leaves. Leaves with a smaller _s(i_) value can only create locked nodes of height _\>k_. Invariant (5) creates one or two additional locked nodes. Thus, for every integer _k_, there are at most \(2\cdot(2^{k+1}-1)+2\le 2^{k+2}\) locked nodes of height \(\le k\).

Consider the state of the main tree after running cleanupStep(_i_). Let _s,t,u,v,w_ be consecutive leaders and let _p_ be the parent of _u_. Suppose that _u_ is not locked and that \(height(u)<4\cdot 2^i\). If moreover \(min(height(s),height(t),height(v),height(w))\ge height(u)\), then _p_ would get activated during cleanupStep(_i_). But _p_ was not activated, thus, one of the leaders _s,t,v,w_ has height at most height(_u_)-1. To summarize: for a leader _u_ of height \(<4\cdot 2^i\) that is not locked, there is a<tbc>

<tbc>leader of lower height within at most two steps to the left or right. By applying this argument inductively, we find a locked leader within at most 2height(_u_) steps from _u_. Thus, for every \(k<4\cdot 2^i\), all leaders of height \(\le k\) are within 2_k_ steps from a locked node of height \(\le k\). As there are 2<sup>_k_+2</sup> such locked nodes, the total number of leaders of height \(\le k\) is bounded by \((4k+1)\cdot 2^{k+2}\le 16\cdot 4^k\).

Let \(1\le j<i\) be arbitrary. By (7), the index tree _L<sub>j</sub>_ contains only leaders of height \(\le 2^{j+2}\). Thus, by the first part of the proof, \(|L_j|\le 16\cdot 4^{2^{j+2}}\). To analyze the size of _L<sub>i</sub>_, we also need to bound the number of leaders of height exactly \(4\cdot 2^i\). In the first step of cleanupStep(_i_), we promote all leaders of height \(4\cdot 2^i\) to _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>. Afterwards, we can only create a leader of height \(4\cdot 2^i\) by destroying two leaders of height \(4\cdot 2^i-1\). By (6), we started with \(\sum_{j=0}^i23\cdot 4^{2^{j+2}}\le 24\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\) leaders, so we created at most \(12\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\) leaders of height exactly \(4\cdot 2^i\). As there are at most \(16\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}-1}=4\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\) leaders of height \(\le 4\cdot 2^i-1\), this shows \(|L_i|\le 16\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\).

**Lemma 22.** _Let i be the maximum index with_ \(|L_i|\ge 20\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\)_. After_ cleanupStep(_i), all invariants hold, with the following refinement for (6): We have_ \(|L_j|\le 20\cdot 4^{2^{j+2}}\) _for all_ \(j\neq i+1\)_, and_ \(|L_{i+1}|\le 23\cdot 4^{2^{(i+1)+2}}\).

_Proof._ Invariant (1) holds since we never activate or deactivate leaves, and Invariant (2) holds since we only ever activate the parent of two leaders. If _t,u,v,w_ are consecutive leaders where _u,v_ have the same parent _p_, then we only activate _p_ if \(height(p)\le min(height(t),height(w))+1\). Thus, invariant (3) holds. We explicitly check for invariants (4) and (5), so these hold too. Lemma 21 shows that invariant (6) holds for \(j\le i\). For \(j\ge i+2\), we do not change _L<sub>j</sub>_ at all, so \(|L_j|\le 20\cdot 4^{2^{j+2}}\) by maximality of _i_. We only change _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>, by promoting leaders from _L<sub>i</sub>_. Thus, \(|L_{i+1}|\le 23\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}+20\cdot 4^{2^{(i+1)+2}}\le 21\cdot 4^{2^{(i+1)+2}}\) by maximality of _i_. This shows the refinement of invariant (6). When rebuilding the index trees, we place the leaders of height \((2\cdot 2^j,4\cdot 2^j]\) into _L<sub>j</sub>_. Thus, invariants (7) and (8) hold.

**Lemma 23.** _The amortized running time of_ cleanupStep(_i_) _is zero._

_Proof._ We first show that cleanupStep(_i_) does not create any bills: Moving leaders to _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub> has no effect on the number of bills. For consecutive leaders _t,u,v,w_ where _u,v_ have the same parent _p_, we only activate _p_ if \(height(p)\le min(height(t),height(w))+1\). Thus, this activation does not create any bills either.

Next, we analyze the number of coins. Let _N_ be the total size of _L_<sub>0</sub>_,...,L<sub>i</sub>_ at the start of cleanupStep(_i_), and let \(N'\) be the total size of _L_<sub>0</sub>_,...,L<sub>i</sub>_ at the end of cleanupStep(_i_). We claim that \(N-N'\in\Omega(N)\). We have \(N\ge 20\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\) since we only run cleanupStep(_i_) if \(|L_i|\ge 20\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\). And, by Lemma 21, we have \(N'\le\sum_{j=0}^i16\cdot 4^{2^{j+2}}\le 17\cdot 4^{2^{i+2}}\). Thus, \(N'\le\frac{17}{20}N\), so \(N-N'\ge\frac{3}{20}N\).

For every leader _u_ that we move to _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>, we get one coin since _u_ stops being unpromoted. Also, whenever we activate a node _p_ with children _u,v_, we get at least one coin. Indeed, we get four coins for destroying the leaders _u,v_, but we need two or three coins for the new leader _p_, depending on whether _p_ is unpromoted. These are the only two operations that decrease the total size of _L_<sub>0</sub>_,...,L<sub>i</sub>_. Thus, we get at least \(N-N'\ge\frac{3}{20}N\) coins in total. In particular, during cleanupStep(_i_), we may spend _O(N_) time for free.

When promoting leaders from _A_ to _L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>, we always promote a block of \(\Omega(2^i)\) leaders. Bulk inserting these leaders takes _O_(log|_L_<sub>_i_+1</sub>|) time, plus constant time per leader. By (6), \(log|L_{i+1}|\in O(2^i)\). Thus, we spend constant time per promoted leader, so _O(N_) time in total.

Afterwards, we activate some nodes, and rebuild the trees _L_<sub>0</sub>_,...,L<sub>i</sub>_. Since every node in the main tree stores its height and the maximum access time of a leaf in its subtree, we can check in<tbc>

_O_(1) time whether a given parent _p_ can be activated. Whenever we do activate _p_, the size of the linked list shrinks by one, so this happens _O(N_) times. We also spend _O(N_) time scanning through the linked list, moving the pointer to _t_, and unsuccessfully activating nodes. Building a balanced binary tree takes linear time in its size. Thus, rebuilding _L_<sub>0</sub>_,...,L<sub>i</sub>_ takes _O(N_) time.

**Theorem 24.** Cleanup _maintains all invariants, has an amortized running time of O_(1)_, and restores the stronger bound in invariant (6)._

_Proof._ Cleanup only modifies the data structure via cleanupStep. By Lemma 22, cleanupStep maintains all invariants. And cleanup only terminates once the stronger bound in invariant (6) holds for all index trees. Thus, all invariants are maintained.

Cleanup spends _O_(1) time checking whether there are any index trees that are too big, in which case it performs a cleanupStep. This is repeated until no cleanupStep happens. If cleanup performs at least one cleanupStep, then the _O_(1) overhead of cleanup is dominated by the time spent in cleanupStep, so the amortized running time of cleanup is zero by Lemma 23. If no cleanupStep happens, then the running time of cleanup is _O_(1).

### 5.8 Putting things together

After every addLeaf or access operation, we run cleanup. We show that our construction achieves Theorem 12:

**Theorem 12.** _There is a data structure that maintains a rooted binary tree on top of n leaves numbered_ 1_,...,n that each store an item, such that each node in the tree stores its subtree minimum and every leaf i has depth O(d(i_))_. The data structure supports the operations:_

• addLeaf(_x): In amortized O_(1) _time, increment n and add a new leaf with index n, value x, and_ \(s(n)=-\infty\).<tbc>

• access(_i): In amortized O(d(i_)) _time (computed before the operation), set s(i_)=_t and then increment t. For the very first access operation, d(i_) _is ill-defined, so we require a bound of amortized O_(1) _time instead._<tbc>

• changeKey(_i,x): In O(d(i_)) _time, replace the item stored at leaf i with x._

_The data structure may remodel the internal tree nodes arbitrarily (within the allowed time bounds). The leaves do not need to be stored in order._

_Proof._ By Lemmas 14 and 15 every leaf _i_ has depth _O(d(i_)). By Theorem 20, addLeaf runs in amortized _O_(1) time. By Lemma 19, access runs in amortized _O(d(i_)) time. By Theorem 24, running cleanup after these operations does not increase the amortized running time. Since the values of items have no effect on the structure of our heap, we only need to update the subtree minima during changeKey. This takes worst case _O(d(i_)) time. Since we run cleanup after every addLeaf or access operation, Lemma 18 and Theorems 20 and 24 show that we maintain all invariants.

## 6 A Slightly Stronger Unified Bound

There are multiple slightly different ways of defining the working set property of heaps \[9, 14, 17\]. The simplest one is that \(x\leftarrow\text{extractMin}()\) takes _O_(log_k_) time where _k_ is the number insert operations while _x_ is in the heap. In the stronger, but more complicated definition, of Elmasry \[9\],<tbc>

the value _k_ only counts insert operations for which the inserted item remains in the heap until _x_ is extracted. In other words, the value _k_ skips items that are extracted before _x_ is extracted.

We designed Definition 1 to be a simple version of the unified bound for Heaps which is sufficient for our result on sorting under partial information. However, our heap construction can be adapted to achieve a stronger but more complicated version of the unified bound. Recall that we consider a sequence of insert and extractMin operations where an item _x_ is the _a(x_)-th item to be inserted and the _b(x_)-th item to be extracted. We modify Definition 1 and decrease the term |_a(x_)-_a(y_)| by only counting items inserted between _x_ and _y_ that are still in the heap. This yields:

**Definition 25.** _A heap data structure has the_ immediate unified bound _if it supports_ insert(_x_) _in amortized O_(1) _time, the very first_ extractMin _operation in amortized O_(1) _time, and subsequent_ \(x\leftarrow\text{extractMin}()\) _operations in amortized time_

\(O\big(min_{y\in Xb(y)<b(x)}\big(1+log|A(x,y)|+log(b(x)-b(y))\big)\big),\)

_where_ \(A(x,y):=\{z\in X|b(z)\ge b(x)\wedge min(a(x),a(y))\le a(z)\le max(a(x),a(y))\}\).

We sketch how the construction in Section 5 can be adapted to the immediate unified bound. This time, we consider up to _n_ leaves, numbered by some subsequence of \[_n_\]. Non-existent numbers correspond to leaves that have been deleted. Let _t_ be a time counter that starts at 0. Every integer \(i\in[n]\) has a last access time _s(i)\<t_. We define \(\overline{d}(i):=1+min_{1\le j\le n}(log(1+|\{k|\text{leaf}k\text{exists}\wedge min(i,j)\le k\le max(i,j)\}|+log(1+t-s(j)))\). Note that every integer _j_ can be used as a finger, even if no leaf _j_ exists.

**Theorem 26.** _\[Improved Theorem 12\] There is a data structure that maintains a rooted binary tree on top of up to n leaves numbered by some subsequence of_ \[_n_\] _that each store an item, such that each node in the tree stores its subtree minimum and every leaf i has depth O_(<o>_d_</o>(_i_))_. The data structure supports the operations, where i is an integer for which a leaf exists:_

• addLeaf(_x): In amortized O_(1) _time, increment n and add a new leaf with index n, value x, and_ \(s(n)=-\infty\).<tbc>

• access(_i): In amortized O_(<o>_d_</o>(_i_)) _time (computed before the operation), set s(i_)=_t and then increment t. For the very first access operation,_ <o>_d_</o>(_i_) _is ill-defined, so we require a bound of amortized O_(1) _time instead._<tbc>

• changeKey(_i,x): In O_(<o>_d_</o>(_i_)) _time, replace the item stored at leaf i with x._<tbc>

• deleteLeaf(_i): In O_(<o>_d_</o>(_i_)) _time, delete the leaf i._

_The data structure may remodel the internal tree nodes arbitrarily (within the allowed time bounds). The leaves do_ not _need to be stored in order._

Given Theorem 26, we obtain a heap with the immediate unified bound (Definition 25) as before, except that extractMin invokes deleteLeaf(_i_) instead of changeKey\((i,\infty)\).

## 6.1 Modifying our Heap Construction

We briefly sketch the changes necessary to go from Theorem 12 to Theorem 26. We call an integer \(i\in[n]\) _alive_ if the leaf _i_ still exists, and _dead_ otherwise. Each leaf of the main tree corresponds to an integer in \[_n_\] that is either dead or alive, but among two consecutive leaves, we require at least<tbc>

<tbc>one of them to be alive. In fact, for every maximal block of consecutive dead integers, we only store the most recently accessed integer as a leaf in the main tree. We also store all alive integers. This ensures that, for any two integers _i,j_, the number of leaves in the main tree with integers between _i_ and _j_ is at most \(2\cdot|\{k|\text{leaf}k\text{exists}\wedge min(i,j)\le k\le max(i,j)\}|\), which then yields the stronger bound <o>_d_</o>(_i_) instead of _d(i_).

For the main tree, we use a 2-3-4 tree \[16\] instead of a complete binary tree. This will allow us to delete leaves corresponding to consecutive dead integers created by the deleteLeaf operation. The index trees remain the same, but the constants in invariant (6) need to be increased since 2-3-4 trees allow nodes to have up to four children. Similarly, some constants in the analysis need to be increased, e.g. in Lemma 17, we may get four consecutive newly created leaders of the same height, and in the proof of Lemma 21, we might need 6height(_u_) steps from _u_ to find a locked leader.

The implementations of addLeaf, access, changeKey, cleanupStep and cleanup remain largely the same. To perform deleteLeaf(_i_), we first invoke \(\text{changeKey}(i,\infty)\). Then, we mark leaf _i_ as dead and delete any adjacent dead leaves in the main tree. This might cause the 2-3-4 tree to perform some rebalancing operations, specifically _fusing_ and _borrowing_ \[16\]. Rebalancing non-leader nodes is a non-issue. For any rebalancing operation involving one or more leader nodes, we first deactivate these leader nodes and perform the operation. Then, we fix invariant (3) as in the access operation, and update the index trees. If _h_ is the height of the node involved in the rebalancing operation, then deactivating leaders creates _O_(1) bills, fixing invariant (3) takes zero amortized time, and updating the index trees takes _O(h_) time. Thus, the amortized running time of a rebalancing operation at height _h_ is _O(h_). The 2-3-4 tree analysis (Theorem 2.b in \[16\]) shows that _n_ insertions and deletions trigger at most \(n\cdot(\frac{3}{5})^{h-1}\) rebalancing operations at height _h_. Thus, the total additional running time due to rebalancing is \(n\cdot\sum_{h=1}^{log_2n}h(\frac{3}{5})^{h-1}\in O(n)\).

## 7 Open problems

### 7.1 Heaps with the Unified Bound

Both the construction and analysis of our heap with the unified bound is complicated and uses a slew of invariants and amortization potentials. It would be nice to have a simple construction, as was achieved for the working set heap \[31\]. Alternatively, it would be interesting to show that an existing self-adjusting structure, such as the smooth heap or pairing heap does the trick.

### 7.2 Chain-Antichain Partition for Points

An earlier attempt at solving sorting under partial information with merge sort (instead of heap sort) failed since we could not solve the following subproblem: You are given an integer _k\>_0 and a list _X_ of _n_ items. In _O(n_log_k_) time, partition _X_ into

• up to _k_ increasing subsequences of any length,<tbc>

• plus any number of decreasing subsequences, each of length at least _k_+1.

Such a partition always exists: While the longest decreasing subsequence of _X_ is longer than _k_, delete it. Afterwards, by Dilworth’s theorem, _X_ can be partitioned into _k_ increasing subsequences.

For our purpose, it would be enough if the decreasing subsequences had length \(\Omega(k^\varepsilon)\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\). The difficult part is that there is no wiggle room in terms of running time: it has to be _O(n_log_k_). (The chain-antichain merge sort of \[19\] solves a generalization of this problem to arbitrary partial orders in \(\tilde{O}(nk^2)\) time.)
